rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: ❌ Heat and temperature are the same thing. ✅ Temperature is the average molecular kinetic energy (intensive). Heat is the total energy transferred (extensive). A spark at 2000°C has tiny heat content; a bathtub at 40°C has huge heat content.  ·  ❌ A body "contains" heat. ✅ A body contains internal energy (kinetic + potential of its molecules). Heat is the TRANSFER of energy due to temperature difference. Once energy is in the body, it's no longer "heat." Think of it like "payment" - once received, it's no longer a payment; it's just money in your account.

rows.label: Limitation
rows.text: ❌ All materials heat up at the same rate with the same power. ✅ Different materials have different specific heats. 1 kW heats 1 kg of aluminum ($c=900$) much faster than 1 kg of water ($c=4200$). The aluminum's temperature rises ~4.7× faster.  ·  ❌ The formula H = mcΔθ works for phase changes too. ✅ This formula ONLY works when temperature changes WITHOUT a phase change. During melting (ice → water at 0°C) or boiling (water → steam at 100°C), temperature stays constant - you need $H = mL$ instead.

rows.label: Universal facts
rows.text: The calorie was originally defined as the heat needed to raise 1 gram of water by 1°C - specifically from 14.5°C to 15.5°C, since water's specific heat varies slightly with temperature. The modern value is $1\text{ cal} = 4.184\text{ J}$ (exact).  ·  Water's anomalously high specific heat ($4200\text{ J/kg·K}$) is due to hydrogen bonding. Breaking these bonds requires extra energy, so more heat goes into the system without raising temperature. This is why oceans moderate Earth's climate.

rows.label: Study notes
rows.text: **Heat is energy in transit:** Heat ($H$) is the thermal energy transferred between systems due to a temperature difference. It is NOT a property of a body - you cannot say "a body contains heat." A body contains internal energy; heat is the transfer of that energy.  ·  **Mass dependency (H ∝ m):** For a given substance and temperature change, the heat required is directly proportional to the mass: $H \propto m$. Doubling the mass doubles the heat needed. This is because more molecules means more total kinetic energy must change.  ·  **Temperature dependency (H ∝ Δθ):** For a given mass, heat is directly proportional to the temperature change: $H \propto \Delta\theta$, where $\Delta\theta = \theta_f - \theta_i$ (final − initial). Heating water from 20°C to 80°C requires 3× the heat of heating from 20°C to 40°C.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Concept 5: Connection between Change of Phases and Latent Heat and other topics  ·  ❌ Specific heat capacity depends on the amount of substance. ✅ Specific heat capacity is an INTENSIVE property - it depends only on the MATERIAL, not the mass. 1 kg of copper has $c = 390\text{ J/kg·K}$, same as 1 g of copper.  ·  ❌ Heat always flows from hot to cold, so a cold object can never lose heat to a hot one. ✅ Heat naturally flows from hot to cold. However, a refrigerator CAN move heat from cold to hot - but only by doing external work (compressor). This doesn't violate the second law.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: ❌ If you add heat, temperature always rises. ✅ During a phase change (melting, boiling, sublimation), added heat goes into breaking intermolecular bonds (increasing potential energy), NOT increasing kinetic energy. Temperature stays constant during the transition.  ·  Carefully distinguish between similar-looking concepts in change of phases and latent heat.  ·  Pay attention to the conditions under which formulas and theorems apply.
